🚨 Threat Actor Claims Breach of Pratt & Whitney, Demands Ransom for Engine Data  An unidentified threat actor has claimed to have breached the internal systems of Pratt & Whitney, a major American aerospace manufacturer, and stolen sensitive technical documentation related to aircraft engines. According to a post on an underground forum, the actor alleges they accessed the company’s headquarters in East Hartford, Connecticut, and exfiltrated highly sensitive maintenance and inspection reports.  The post details the theft of specific documents concerning engine V10519 of the V2527 A5 model, which is used on Airbus A320 aircraft. The alleged stolen data includes: *   Engine receipt reports and installed accessories reports containing part numbers (P/N) and serial numbers (S/N). *   Borescope inspection reports and engine disassembly reports. *   Detailed status of oil systems, fuel filters, sensors, and air valves. *   Maintenance schedules and functional inspection results for solenoid valves.  The actor claims the specific engine belongs to customer IAE FHA / Kingfisher and is registered to aircraft VT ADZ, with 18,781 operating hours and 11,313 cycles. The report allegedly prepared by Peter J Mahan at the Christchurch Engine Centre in New Zealand in 2009 is cited as evidence of the breach. The threat actor asserts that this data poses a risk to US national security by potentially enabling industrial espionage or targeting aviation supply chains.  Pratt & Whitney, a subsidiary of RTX Corporation (formerly United Technologies Corporation), is one of the world’s leading manufacturers of aircraft engines, supplying both military platforms like the F-35 and F-22, and commercial fleets. The actor is demanding a financial ransom within 72 hours to prevent the sale of these documents to hostile nations or rival manufacturers. If the demand is not met, they threaten to auction the data on dark web markets.  At the time of reporting, Pratt & Whitney has not publicly confirmed the incident, and the authenticity of the leaked technical documents remains unverified. The claimant’s identity and operational history are unknown, and no independent corroboration of the breach has been established.  #PrattWhitney #AerospaceSecurity #DataBreach #Ransomware #DarkWeb #CyberSecurity

🚨 Threat Actor Claims Full Compromise of Bangladesh Army Network  A darkweb forum post alleges that the internal network of the Bangladesh Army, specifically the Qadirabad Cantonment headquarters, has been fully compromised. The anonymous actor claims to have gained unauthorized access to a primary MikroTik CCR1036-8G-2S+ router (IP: 27.147.148.184) running an outdated version of RouterOS (6.49.18), exploiting exposed SNMP, Winbox, and SSH services to map the entire infrastructure.  According to the listing, the breach exposes critical operational details of the military base, including: *   A complete network map revealing over 50 internal subnets and more than 400 live devices. *   Backup files containing plaintext passwords and RADIUS configurations with weak credentials (e.g., "123321"). *   User login logs and system diagnostic files (autosupout.rif). *   A list of over 100 active PPPoE connections and MAC addresses of connected servers, computers, and VoIP phones.  The post details specific vulnerabilities exploited on the main device, including CVE-2018-14847 in Winbox and unpatched flaws in SSH and SNMP. The actor claims access to sensitive interfaces connected to service provider Link3 Technologies and VLANs labeled for various military functions (e.g., vlan2402-GGC, vlan2403-FNA). Additionally, the hotspot folder containing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files used for the wireless internet portal was allegedly extracted, which could potentially be leveraged to compromise connected users.  The Bangladesh Army is a major national security force, and Qadirabad Cantonment serves as a significant logistical and administrative hub. While the technical details provided in the post are specific, including file names like 15123_1812358-20260513-2247.backup and precise interface statistics, the incident remains unverified by official sources. If authentic, the exposure of internal routing tables and device credentials could enable further lateral movement or targeted attacks against military communications infrastructure.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified.  #BangladeshArmy #DataBreach #MikroTik #NetworkSecurity #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence #MilitaryCyberSecurity

The anonymous actor alleges that the data was extracted from the military's internal systems and includes sensitive operational files, recruitment records, and intelligence reports.  The listing details a vast array of leaked artifacts, categorized into general IDF documents and specific files attributed to Unit 8200. The actor claims the dump contains hundreds of PDFs, Word documents, and converted files. Notable categories of alleged leaked material include:  *   **Unit 8200 Intelligence Files:** A subdirectory labeled "Signal Intelligence Unit 8200" allegedly contains 1987 items in "Original format," including numerous PDFs and .docx files with sequential ID numbers. *   **Recruitment and HR Records:** Files named with prefixes such as "AllJobs_" and "CV_From_" suggest the exposure of job postings and candidate resumes, potentially revealing internal hiring processes or personnel data. *   **General Administrative Documents:** A large collection of files with alphanumeric identifiers (e.g., "119534_638079043105431895.pdf") is listed under a general "Leaked documents" section.  Unit 8200 is widely regarded as one of the world's most advanced signals intelligence units, responsible for electronic warfare, cyber operations, and code-breaking. The IDF is the primary armed forces organization of Israel, tasked with national defense. If authentic, the exposure of internal communications and intelligence methodologies could have significant implications for national security and operational security (OPSEC). However, no independent verification has been provided by the IDF or cybersecurity researchers at this time.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified. ⚠️ Threat Actor Claims Massive Leak of US Law Enforcement and Intelligence Databases  An anonymous threat actor has posted a claim on an underground forum alleging the theft of extensive data from multiple United States federal law enforcement and intelligence agencies. The post, dated September 25, 2026, asserts that the actor possesses "all CIA correspondence from 2000 to the present" as well as classified FBI and Secret Service communications dating back to 2016 and 2019, respectively.  According to the listing, the alleged data dump includes highly sensitive materials such as: *   Classified White House documents from 2020 to the present *   Dossiers on individuals under FBI and CIA surveillance *   Complete personnel files for officers handling espionage and counter-espionage cases *   Audio recordings of over 700,000 individuals accused of espionage, murder, and cybercrimes *   All US police records and data from over 10 million case files  The actor provides a link to a website (mrhex.sbs) for viewing "live photos" and a file host link purportedly containing the 10 million case files. No independent verification of these claims has been provided by the Department of Justice, FBI, CIA, or other relevant federal agencies. Claims of such magnitude involving core national security databases are frequently used in phishing scams or as disinformation tactics by unverified actors; however, if authentic, the exposure would represent a catastrophic compromise of US national security infrastructure.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified. Federal agencies have not issued public statements confirming or denying the incident.

🚨 HSRgroup Claims SQL Injection Breach of Indian Government Services  A threat actor operating under the alias HSRgroup has posted a claim on an underground forum alleging a large-scale data breach of multiple Indian government services. According to the post, the data was obtained through SQL injection attacks targeting official government portals. The actor claims to have compromised the Copyright Office of India (copyright.gov.in), the National Health Mission Uttar Pradesh portal (ekavach.nhm.up.gov.in), and the Central GST Vadodara Zone system (cgstvadodarazone.gov.in).  The post details specific data exposures across these three targets: copyright.gov.in: Allegedly 90 files containing accounts, passwords, sessions, OTPs, personal participant data, and financial records. The actor claims this includes 738,000 lines with email addresses, 655,000 records with full names and addresses, and 184,000 MD5-hashed login credentials. ekavach.nhm.up.gov.in: A file named data.json allegedly containing 939,438 unique strings, including Aadhaar IDs, employee names, mobile phone numbers, and school coordinator records. cgstvadodarazone.gov.in: Access to a CRM system using superadmin credentials. The actor claims access to 66 database files including employee accounts, organizational structure, payment gateways, and system logs.  The post includes sample data rows showing full names, addresses, and contact details for individuals associated with educational institutions in Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, as well as a list of government email addresses paired with plaintext passwords for the GST system. sample_tweets.text: 🔎 OSINT INVESTIGATION PLAYBOOK  Good OSINT is not about collecting more clues.  It is about turning clues into intelligence through structure, validation, and disciplined analysis.  This playbook walks through a practical investigation workflow, including:  * Defining the objective before you search * Starting with simple pivots like usernames, screenshots, domains, and IPs * Expanding into GitHub, DNS, and historical infrastructure * Extracting intelligence from screenshots, metadata, and reverse image search * Using geolocation and social media correlation to test possible links * Building timelines to understand what happened, when, and in what order * Returning to the original document to uncover overlooked pivots * Comparing multiple evidence chains instead of relying on a single clue  Most importantly, it reinforces one of the biggest lessons in OSINT:  ⚠️ Correlation is not attribution.  A matching username, similar profile photo, shared city, or linked domain may suggest a connection, but none of them alone prove identity or responsibility.  Analyst Note:  Strong OSINT does not try to prove a theory.  It tries to break it.  The best investigators:  * Preserve originals * Document every source * Verify with multiple independent indicators * Challenge assumptions * Look for contradictions * Build timelines * Revisit earlier evidence * Ask: “What would prove me wrong?”  Search less. Think more. Verify everything.  #DDW #OSINT #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity #OpenSourceIntelligence #DigitalInvestigation #Geolocation #Metadata #Forensics

Microsoft made MicrosoftDocs/memdocs private. 😠  If you track Intune documentation changes, that repo was how you did it. It is 404 now. Not archived, not moved. Gone.  The important part: the docs themselves are fine. Every Intune and Autopilot page still publishes on Microsoft Learn exactly as before. What disappeared was the public git history behind them, and with it every diff, every page history, and every answer to "what actually changed on this page last Tuesday."  That broke Daily Intune News, which I build from that history. Intune just went dark.  I don't like it when Microsoft tells me 'No'.  So here's my workaround 🥰  I crawl the published Learn pages, save each one as Markdown at the path Learn built it from, and commit only what genuinely changed. The history of the crawl becomes the history of the docs.  intune-docs-mirror, the result for Intune and Autopilot.
